newsitem.title: USA: Official sees US Q1 consumer spending down from Q4.
newsitem.headline: Official sees US Q1 consumer spending down from Q4.

text.p: A top U.S. Commerce Department official predicted Thursday that first quarter growth in consumer spending will be weaker than the last quarter of 1996, but stronger than the third quarter.

"When we look at the first quarter ... the consumer sector will not be as strong as it was in the fourth quarter but will nonetheless be stronger than we saw in the third quarter," Everett Ehrlich, underscrecretary for economic affairs at the Commerce Department, said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
Ehrlich was commenting on retail sales figures which showed improvement in January, up from December figures which were much weaker than previously reported.
Ehrlich also said that he expected no problem with inflation in coming months.
"We should see stability in both the labor market and prices of final products in the several months ahead," he said.
But he cautioned that there might be some tendency to overestimate inflation in the first few months of the year because of flawed measurement techniques.

Ehrlich said he thought the effect of the revision of December retail sales -- originally reported at 0.6 but revised Thursday to 0.3 percent -- would make no more than a 0.1 pct difference in the GDP.
"I think the larger revision we see in the fourth quarter GDP comes from the fact that wholesale inventories as reported a few days ago were lower than we thought they might have been," he said.

One analyst said the fact that there were back-to-back increases in retail spending of any size was in itself significant. The report for January showed an overall increase of 0.6 percent in retail sales.

"This month's data marks the first time since mid-1995 that we had had back-to-back monthly increases in retail spending," said Bernice Behar, senior vice president and portfolio manager at John Hancock Funds. She said in a statement the mild winter and low inflation contributed to the increased spending.
